design_detail: Case-control analysis of records from the US Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS), 1991 to 2008: drivers aged 20 or older of cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks who were in a fatal crash and had a blood alcohol result and at least one blood drug test. Cases were drivers with at least one recorded potentially unsafe driver action (UDA; FARS driver-related factors 20 to 60, for example weaving), controls drivers with none, so the comparison is among drivers already in a fatal crash and the UDA is the authors' proxy for responsibility; it is not a comparison with drivers who did not crash. Logistic regression built in four steps (Models 1 to 4, with a step-down procedure); the final model has age (linear and quadratic), sex, blood alcohol concentration (BAC; linear and quadratic), THC (any positive test), a THC-by-BAC term, age-by-sex and age-by-BAC terms, other drug classes (depressants, narcotics, stimulants, other) and the previous three-year driving record (crashes, drink or drug driving convictions, speeding, other convictions, licence suspensions). Predicted odds and odds ratios were computed from the final model for male drivers aged 45 (Table 3). A secondary analysis used 1,004 drivers with two or three THC-positive tests (1993 to 2008). Read as the journal's accepted manuscript (not the typeset article); Appendix 1 is not in the PDF.
can_establish: How the odds that a driver in a fatal US crash had a police-recorded unsafe action differed with blood alcohol, a THC-positive blood test and both, after adjustment for age, sex, other drugs and driving record, and how the THC association changed as blood alcohol rose (negative THC-by-BAC term).
cannot_establish: Crash risk (every driver studied was in a fatal crash); impairment, timing or amount of cannabis use (THC is a yes/no blood marker); causation; non-fatal crashes; drivers who were not blood tested for both alcohol and drugs (about four in five eligible drivers); or, with a printed test, that THC adds to alcohol at BAC .05 or .08.

sample.recruitment: Registry: FARS, compiled by the National Center for Statistics and Analysis of the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration; all drivers in the 1991 to 2008 files who met the criteria; details of the source are in an earlier paper by the authors (Methods › Data Source, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: drivers of passenger cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks; age 20 or older (younger drivers left out because they would not have had enough driving history); a valid blood alcohol content from a blood test (FARS range 0 to .94 g/dL); at least one confirmed blood drug test. Left out: 47 drivers with sex not coded, 397,396 not blood tested for alcohol, 174,814 blood tested for alcohol but not for drugs, and, from the primary analyses, 1,004 drivers with two or three THC-positive tests. A comparison of the three testing groups is said to be in Appendix 1, which is not in the manuscript PDF (Methods › Inclusion Criteria; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (alcohol- and THC-free, alcohol only, THC only, THC plus alcohol): mean age 46.5 (SD 19.2), 35.7 (13.1), 32.5 (11.4), 30.7 (9.6) years; male 64.3%, 82.5%, 78.8%, 85.2%; previous drink or drug driving conviction 1.8%, 10.6%, 4.5%, 11.8%; licence suspension 9.8%, 26.0%, 26.8%, 33.0%; stimulants 5.0%, 8.9%, 21.0%, 15.5%; any other drug class 15.4%, 18.1%, 37.0%, 27.1%. Race, ethnicity, vehicle, time of day and place are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records), but only 150,010 of 722,220 eligible drivers (20.8%, editors' calculation) had both blood tests: 55.0% had no blood alcohol test and 24.2% a blood alcohol test without a drug test. The four exposure groups add to 149,006; the other 1,004 of the 150,010 were outside the primary analyses (editors' arithmetic). Previous-record variables are missing for 1.6% to 7.8% of drivers (Table 1 footnote); how missing values were handled is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Selection into testing: which drivers get blood alcohol and drug tests depends on state practice, on the driver surviving and probably on police suspicion, and testing for drugs rose from about 30% of alcohol-tested drivers in 1991 to about 70% in 2008. The authors adjust the prevalence trend for this but do not discuss selection into testing as a limit on the odds ratios. Everyone studied was in a fatal crash, so the findings concern drivers in fatal crashes in the United States, and the comparison group is crashed drivers without a recorded unsafe action, not drivers in general (Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 1st and 5th paragraphs).

exposure.measurement: Blood (serum) tests recorded in FARS: alcohol as BAC in g/dL, and THC as any positive result among eight THC-containing drug codes (delta-9, hashish oil, hashish, marijuana, Marinol, tetrahydrocannabinoid, THC, cannabinoid of unknown type). Drugs were recorded by group in 1991 and 1992 and individually from 1993, with up to three serum analyses per driver. Whether a positive result means parent THC or an inactive metabolite is not stated, and no concentration is recorded (Methods › Cannabis, and other drug classification and exposure; Discussion, 5th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded: FARS has no route of administration, no blood concentration at the time of the crash and no dose, so THC is a yes/no marker; the authors note THC can stay in the blood for hours or even days. Time between use and the crash is unknown (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug classes (depressants, narcotics, stimulants, other: hallucinogens, PCP, anabolic steroids, inhalants) enter the final model as separate terms. Among the 7,734 THC-positive drivers, 56% (4,347) also had alcohol, 31% (2,433) another drug and 18% (1,386) a stimulant. Alcohol is modelled by BAC with linear and quadratic terms and a THC-by-BAC term (Results, 5th paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: tests were taken after the crash; time since use is not available.

comparison.controls: Drivers who were themselves in a fatal crash and had no unsafe driver action recorded, a stand-in for drivers who did not contribute to the crash. For the exposure, the reference is a driver with BAC 0.00 and no THC detected.
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment for age (linear and quadratic), sex, other drug classes and the previous three-year driving record, with age-by-sex and age-by-BAC terms (Methods › Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Risk-taking and the reasons for THC use: the previous driving record is the authors' stand-in for risk-taking. FARS does not say why THC was present, and therapeutic use or underlying conditions (for example sleep or musculoskeletal disorders) may account for part of the association (Discussion, 5th paragraph). Time of day, road, vehicle and number of vehicles are not in the final model (Table 2).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other drug classes adjusted for: depressants OR 1.55, narcotics 1.33, stimulants 1.84, other 1.15 (Table 2).

outcomes.instruments: At least one FARS unsafe driver action (driver-related factors 20 to 60; police-recorded actions that may have contributed to starting the crash) as a yes/no proxy for responsibility; the manuscript gives weaving as the only example (Methods › Proxy measure of responsibility).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors say UDAs are preferred to traffic violations, which can be under-recorded, and that in crash configurations where responsibility can be inferred (head-on, rear-end) the driver of the striking vehicle usually gets most UDAs, citing a 1998 report and their own 2013 research-showcase paper; not checked here. The manuscript does not say how alcohol or drug involvement itself is coded.
outcomes.operationalization: The odds that a driver in a fatal crash had a recorded unsafe action for a given BAC and THC status, against a driver with BAC 0.00 and no THC. The paper words this as culpability odds, responsibility and crash risk; it is neither crash risk nor a measure of impairment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated: one outcome, a step-down model-building procedure over age, sex and interaction terms, and a secondary analysis by number of THC-positive tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: administrative records. Police coded unsafe actions at the scene, before laboratory results, but could have known or suspected alcohol or drug involvement; the manuscript does not address this.

analysis.effect_sizes: Final model (Table 2; referent BAC 0.00 and no THC): THC at BAC 0.00, B 0.153 (SE 0.038), OR 1.165 (95% CI 1.082 to 1.255); BAC per 0.01 g/100 mL, B 0.109 (0.002), OR 1.115 (1.110 to 1.120); BAC squared, B -0.002 (0.000), OR 0.998 (0.998 to 0.999); THC-by-BAC, B -0.013 (0.003), OR 0.987 (0.981 to 0.994); depressants 1.553 (1.451 to 1.662), narcotics 1.334 (1.241 to 1.435), stimulants 1.837 (1.734 to 1.945), other 1.149 (1.085 to 1.216); previous crashes (one, two, three or more) 1.128, 1.268, 1.385; suspensions 1.256, 1.329, 1.329; a previous drink or drug driving conviction was not associated (0.954, 1.002, 0.939). Model 1 (THC with linear and quadratic BAC only): THC 1.28 (1.21 to 1.36); BAC from .00 to .01, 1.11 (1.110 to 1.118); the linear THC-by-BAC term was significant in Model 2 (Wald 18.16, P < .001). Male THC-negative drivers, BAC .08 against .00, at ages 20, 40, 60, 80: 1.98, 2.18, 1.99, 1.49. Table 3 (male driver aged 45; predicted odds of a recorded unsafe driver action without THC and with THC; odds ratio against no alcohol and no THC for alcohol alone, B:A, and for alcohol with THC, C:A, with 95% CI): BAC .00: 1.07 and 1.25; B:A 1.00 (not applicable); C:A 1.16 (1.08 to 1.26). BAC .01: 1.19 and 1.37; 1.11 (1.11 to 1.12); 1.28 (1.19 to 1.38). BAC .02: 1.32 and 1.50; 1.24 (1.23 to 1.25); 1.40 (1.31 to 1.50). BAC .03: 1.46 and 1.64; 1.37 (1.35 to 1.38); 1.53 (1.44 to 1.64). BAC .04: 1.61 and 1.79; 1.51 (1.49 to 1.53); 1.67 (1.57 to 1.78). BAC .05: 1.78 and 1.94; 1.66 (1.63 to 1.69); 1.81 (1.70 to 1.93). BAC .06: 1.95 and 2.10; 1.82 (1.78 to 1.86); 1.96 (1.84 to 2.09). BAC .07: 2.13 and 2.27; 1.99 (1.94 to 2.04); 2.12 (1.99 to 2.26). BAC .08: 2.32 and 2.44; 2.17 (2.11 to 2.23); 2.28 (2.13 to 2.44). Editors' calculations from the printed predicted odds (odds divided by one plus the odds): for the reference driver of Table 3 only, about 52 in 100 (51.7%) had a recorded unsafe driver action at BAC .00 with no THC, 56 (55.6%) with THC alone, 64 (64.0%) at BAC .05 and 66 (66.0%) at .05 with THC, 70 (69.9%) at .08 and 71 (70.9%) at .08 with THC. The ratio of predicted odds with THC to those without it at the same BAC is 1.17 at .00, 1.09 at .05 and 1.05 at .08, which matches 1.165 multiplied by 0.987 for each .01 of BAC. The combined odds ratio is close to the sum of the two separate excesses up to BAC .04 (for example .04: 1.51 + 0.165 = 1.68 against 1.67 printed) and a little below it above that (.05: about 1.83 against 1.81; .08: about 2.34 against 2.28), and below the product of the two odds ratios (1.93 at .05; 2.53 at .08). The constant (0.140) and the sex coefficient (-0.074) reproduce the printed 1.07 at BAC .00 only if the other covariates are at their reference values (no other drugs, no previous crashes, convictions or suspensions). Secondary analysis (1993 to 2008, all THC-positive drivers, THC coded 0, 1, 2 or more positive detections): OR 1.18 (1.09 to 1.27) for one and 1.38 (1.13 to 1.68) for two or more; linear trend P = .002, quadratic trend P = .972. Prevalence of any THC detection (Fig 1, read by eye): unadjusted about 1.4% (1991) to 7.9% (2008); adjusted to the 1993 testing rate, about 1.5% (1991) to a maximum of 4.6% (text), above 3% from 1996 and above 3.5% from 2002 (text); THC with alcohol was more common than THC alone in every year.
analysis.covariates: Age and age squared, sex, BAC and BAC squared, THC, THC-by-BAC, age-by-sex, age squared by sex, age-by-BAC, age squared by BAC, depressants, narcotics, stimulants, other drugs, and counts (0, 1, 2, 3 or more) of previous crashes, drink or drug driving convictions, speeding convictions, other convictions and licence suspensions over three years (Table 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The Introduction states two hypotheses: alcohol detection would fall and THC detection rise from 1993 to 2008, and the combination would raise the odds of an unsafe action compared with alcohol- and THC-free drivers (a comparison with alcohol alone is not stated as a hypothesis).
analysis.selective_reporting: The hypothesised fall in alcohol detection has no reported result (Fig 1 shows THC only). The THC-by-BAC term was kept because of a significant Wald test in Model 2 and the final model was reached by a step-down procedure, so the interaction is data-driven. Appendix 1, with a worked example of the predicted odds and the comparison of tested and untested drivers, is not in the manuscript.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the sample is large (7,734 THC-positive drivers), the intervals for the THC odds ratio are narrow, and the intervals for alcohol alone and for the combination overlap at BAC .05 and .08.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among drivers of cars in fatal US crashes (1991 to 2008) who had blood tests for alcohol and drugs, a recorded unsafe driver action was more likely with higher BAC (OR 1.115 per 0.01, flattening slightly) and, at BAC 0.00, with a THC-positive test (adjusted OR 1.165, 1.082 to 1.255; 1.28 with only BAC terms in the model). For a male driver aged 45 with no other drugs or record, the printed odds ratios against no alcohol and no THC are 1.66 (1.63 to 1.69) at BAC .05 and 1.81 (1.70 to 1.93) with THC, and 2.17 (2.11 to 2.23) at .08 and 2.28 (2.13 to 2.44) with THC. The negative THC-by-BAC term (0.987 per 0.01) means the odds ratio for THC shrinks as BAC rises: about 1.17 at .00, 1.09 at .05 and 1.05 at .08 (editors' calculation). The combination is close to the sum of the two separate excesses and below their product.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title is about impact on crash risk and the Highlights speak of culpability odds. The abstract and conclusion say drivers positive for both agents had greater odds of making an error than drivers positive for either one; the Conclusion speaks of the additive effect of cannabis at low BAC, and the Discussion that public health education should consider highlighting the association between low levels of alcohol, cannabis and crash risk. Gaps: (1) the outcome is a recorded unsafe action among drivers already in a fatal crash, not crash risk; (2) THC is a yes/no blood marker of unstated analyte, so impairment and timing are not measured; (3) greater than alcohol alone rests on adjacent, overlapping intervals in Table 3 (1.81 against 1.66 at .05; 2.28 against 2.17 at .08), with no printed test of THC's added effect at those levels, which is about 9% and 5% of the odds (editors' calculation); (4) additive in the Conclusion is not what the model tests, since the product term concerns departure from multiplicative combination; (5) the stated hypothesis compares the combination with alcohol- and THC-free drivers; (6) the Abstract and Discussion give the 2008 THC prevalence as above 10%, against almost 8% in the Results and Fig 1.

timeline.event: Bédard, Dubois and Weaver (Can J Public Health): earlier analysis of FARS by the same group, THC alone 29% higher odds of an unsafe action, as the Discussion cites it; not read.
Asbridge et al. (BMJ): nine studies, pooled odds ratio 1.92 (1.35 to 2.73) for acute cannabis use and collisions, from crude counts; cited in the Introduction; read for this library.

Hartman et al. (Drug Alcohol Depend): driving simulator, 18 adults analysed; effects of THC and alcohol on lane weaving added up with no interaction detected. Different design and outcome; read for this library.

Rogeberg and Elvik (Addiction): meta-analysis of 28 estimates; this paper enters as 1.10 (1.02 to 1.18), the heaviest weight (10.68%), after conversion for the culpability design; pooled 1.36 and 1.22, and 1.11 to 1.18 where alcohol was controlled. Not independent of this paper; read for this library.

replication.where_it_stands: THC alone (adjusted 1.165) sits within the 1.1 to 1.4 range of the 2016 pooled estimates, which contain this study as the largest weight, so the two are not independent; the 2012 pooled 1.92 is higher. For the combination, a small driving-simulator study read for this library (Hartman 2015) also found effects that added up, on a different outcome; the older on-road studies the Introduction cites disagree with each other and were not read. No independent crash-data analysis of THC with low blood alcohol was read.

funding.funder: AUTO21 Network of Centres of Excellence and the Ontario Neurotrauma Foundation (Acknowledgements). The manuscript says nothing about the funders' role.
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated in the accepted manuscript (no declaration of interests section).
funding.affiliations_note: Research Department, St. Joseph's Care Group; Centre for Research on Safe Driving, Lakehead University; Northern Ontario School of Medicine, Thunder Bay, Ontario, Canada. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Roadside or crash-site samples matched on place and time, with blood THC concentration and time since use, so that the comparison is with drivers who did not crash; police coding of the unsafe action made without knowledge of alcohol and drug results; alcohol in bands (none, below .05, .05 to .08) with THC's added odds ratio and its interval printed at each band; the interaction tested on the additive and the multiplicative scale; and a model of who gets tested.

domains.note: The model adjusts for BAC as a measured dose, age, sex, other drug classes and a three-year driving record, the main confounders named. Not in the model: time of day, road, vehicle, speed, and traits that predict both driving after cannabis and unsafe actions beyond the record; no negative-control exposure.

Laboratory blood tests, but THC is a yes/no marker of unstated analyte with no concentration or timing; misclassification of impairment is probably unrelated to the outcome and would pull estimates towards no effect, as the authors say.

Only about one in five eligible drivers had both blood tests; testing depends on state practice, survival and probably suspicion; testing rose from 30% to 70% over the period; the comparison of tested and untested drivers is in an appendix not available. Both groups are drivers in fatal crashes, which conditions on the outcome of the crash.
Not a concern for a blood test taken after a crash.
Previous-record variables are missing for 1.6% to 7.8% of drivers (valid percentages), and handling is not described.

A police-recorded unsafe action is a proxy for responsibility, validated by the authors' own cited work only (striking-vehicle drivers get more UDAs); coding at the scene could be influenced by suspected alcohol or drug involvement, and the factors counted are not listed.

No protocol is mentioned; the interaction term and final model came from a step-down procedure; a stated hypothesis on alcohol detection trends has no reported result; the key contrast of combination against alcohol alone has no printed test.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain, and two domains are judged high: selection into blood testing (about 21% of eligible drivers, with practice changing over the period) and the outcome, a police-coded proxy for responsibility among drivers already in fatal crashes. The study is large and its handling of BAC, other drugs and driving record is careful, and the authors state the main limits of the THC marker. It may be cited for the pattern of odds of a recorded unsafe action by BAC and a THC-positive test among tested drivers in fatal US crashes, for the sub-multiplicative, close to additive pattern of the combination in Table 3 and for the small added odds ratio for THC at BAC .05 to .08 (about 1.09 and 1.05, editors' calculation); it may not be cited for crash risk, impairment, causation, a THC concentration, non-fatal crashes, or the risk to any one driver.

key_findings.finding: Aim and design: to explore the combined influence of low blood alcohol (BAC up to .08) and cannabis on crash risk. Drivers aged 20 or older tested for both drugs and alcohol after a fatal crash in the United States, 1991 to 2008, were examined in a case-control design: cases had at least one potentially unsafe driver action recorded, controls none. Two hypotheses: alcohol detection would fall and THC detection rise over time, and the combination would raise the odds of an unsafe action compared with alcohol- and THC-free drivers.

Data and inclusion: FARS records of drivers of passenger cars, sport-utility vehicles and light trucks, aged 20 or older, with a valid blood alcohol test and at least one confirmed blood drug test. The unsafe-driver-action proxy is preferred to traffic violations, which can be under-recorded, and is supported by the observation that the driver of the striking vehicle usually gets most UDAs.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data Source; Inclusion Criteria; Proxy measure of responsibility

key_findings.finding: Exposure and covariates: eight THC-containing drug codes counted as THC; drugs recorded by group in 1991 and 1992 and individually from 1993, up to three serum analyses per driver; the primary analysis counts drivers with one THC drug positive. Other drug classes and the previous three-year driving record (crashes, drink or drug driving, speeding, other convictions, suspensions) enter the model.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Cannabis, and other drug classification and exposure; Previous Driving History

key_findings.finding: Analysis: Pearson chi-square and analysis of variance for characteristics; prevalence by year, unadjusted and adjusted to the 1993 testing rate; logistic regression in four steps (Model 1 THC with linear and quadratic BAC; Model 2 THC-by-BAC; Model 3 age, sex and their interaction by a step-down procedure; Model 4 final) and predicted odds and odds ratios with 95% intervals from the final model.

Sample: 834,328 drivers of cars in fatal crashes, 722,267 aged 20 or older, 722,220 after dropping 47 without sex; 150,010 were blood tested for alcohol and drugs (397,396 not tested for alcohol, 174,814 tested for alcohol only). Of the 150,010: 87,280 alcohol- and THC-free, 53,992 alcohol only, 3,387 THC only, 4,347 THC with alcohol; 1,004 more had two (909) or three (95) THC-positive tests and were left out of the primary analyses. Drivers positive for alcohol, THC or both were younger, more often male and had poorer driving records; polydrug use was commonest with THC, stimulants the most frequent class.

Prevalence: unadjusted THC detection rose from less than 2% to almost 8% by 2008 (Fig 1 Panel A, about 1.4% in 1991 and 7.9% in 2008 by eye); THC was found with alcohol more often than alone in every year (the authors give an average percentage difference of about 29%, from 7% in 1997 to 44% in 1995). Drug testing of alcohol-tested drivers rose from about 30% to 70%; adjusted to the 1993 rate, detection was relatively stable, from 1.5% in 1991 to as high as 4.6%, above 3% from 1996 and above 3.5% from 2002.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Fig 1 (Panels A and B); Discussion, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Fig 1 values are read by eye from the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol: from BAC .00 to .01 the odds of an unsafe action rose by 11% (Model 1 OR 1.11, 1.110 to 1.118); each later .01 step was slightly smaller (quadratic term 0.99). THC alone with BAC terms only: 28% higher odds (OR 1.28, 1.21 to 1.36); the linear THC-by-BAC interaction was significant (Wald 18.16, P < .001; Model 2).

Final model: age had a curved relation with unsafe actions (highest for the youngest and oldest drivers) and interacted with BAC (for male THC-negative drivers, BAC .08 against .00 gave odds ratios 1.98, 2.18, 1.99 and 1.49 at ages 20, 40, 60 and 80) and with sex. After adjustment, depressants, narcotics, stimulants and other drugs raised the odds of an unsafe action by 55%, 33%, 84% and 15%; one previous crash by 13% and three or more by 39%; one previous suspension by 26% and three or more by 33%.

THC and alcohol in the final model: THC at BAC 0.00, OR 1.165 (1.082 to 1.255); linear BAC OR 1.115 (1.110 to 1.120) and quadratic 0.998 per 0.01; THC-by-BAC OR 0.987 (0.981 to 0.994), which the authors read as the effect of combining the two being greatest at lower BAC.

Predicted odds and odds ratios (male, age 45): see Table 3. At BAC .05 the odds ratio against no alcohol and no THC is 1.66 for alcohol alone and 1.81 (1.70 to 1.93) with THC; at .08, 2.17 and 2.28 (2.13 to 2.44). At BAC 0.00 THC alone gives 1.16 (1.08 to 1.26). Discussion states these as 66% and 117% greater odds for alcohol at .05 and .08 and 81% and 128% with THC.
key_findings.note: Checked on the rendered page. Table 3 is for a 45-year-old man; the other covariates are not stated (editors' check: reference values reproduce 1.07).

key_findings.finding: Fig 2 plots the log odds of an unsafe action by BAC for ages 25, 45 and 65, both sexes, with and without THC; the THC and no-THC lines move closer together as BAC rises (the negative THC-by-BAC term); the slopes with BAC are steepest in middle-aged and younger drivers and flatter at 65. The male age-45 values (log odds 0.07 and 0.22 at BAC 0, 0.84 and 0.89 at .08, by eye) match the natural logs of Table 3 (1.07, 1.25, 2.32, 2.44).

Secondary analysis of the 1,004 drivers with two or more THC-positive tests (1993 to 2008): log odds 1.61, 1.78 and 1.93 for 0, 1 and 2 or more detections at BAC 0; odds ratios 1.18 (1.09 to 1.27) for one and 1.38 (1.13 to 1.68) for two or more; linear trend P = .002 and no quadratic trend (P = .972).

Discussion: prevalence figures resemble other crash studies (4% to 12%); THC alone with BAC 0.00 gave 16% higher odds of an unsafe action, lower than the 29% from the authors' earlier study, which they attribute to a wider age range and a model that accounts for alcohol and other drugs. As BAC rises the impairing effects of alcohol dominate the relationship between THC and alcohol. Among 7,734 THC-positive drivers, 56% had alcohol, 31% another drug and 18% a stimulant.

Limits the authors state: FARS has no route of administration, blood concentration at the time of crash or dose, so THC is a yes/no marker; THC can stay in blood for hours or days, so some THC-positive drivers may not have been impaired, which they say would understate the culpability odds; FARS does not say why THC was present, and therapeutic use or underlying conditions may account for some of the association. Strengths named: number of fatal crashes, control for age, sex, record and other drugs, narrow intervals, exploration of the combination by age, sex and number of THC detections.

Conclusion: drivers positive for both agents had greater odds of making an error than drivers positive for either alone; further research is needed on low to legal BAC levels (.05 and .08), cannabis concentration and specific driving behaviours, to support roadside screening and public health education about the additive effect of cannabis at low BAC. Funded by AUTO21 Network of Centres of Excellence and the Ontario Neurotrauma Foundation.

Background the Introduction gives: research generally suggests the effect of alcohol and cannabis together is additive or possibly synergistic, with some studies finding no additive effect; on-road studies disagree at low alcohol with small cannabis doses (no clear difference in a driving proficiency test in one, severe impairment with the combination but minor to moderate impairment with each alone in another); a 2012 meta-analysis gave a pooled odds ratio of 1.92 for acute cannabis use and collisions.
key_findings.note: Background statements about other studies, not read for this card.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2008 prevalence of THC detection is given as above 10% in the Abstract and Discussion (1st paragraph) but as almost 8% in the Results (2nd paragraph); Fig 1 Panel A shows any THC at about 7.9% in 2008, and no bar reaches 10%. The five-fold rise matches about 1.4% in 1991 and about 7.9% in 2008. The Results also say less than two percent in 1992, while Fig 1 shows about 1.4% in 1991 and about 2.2% in 1992 (by eye).
reporting_issues.consequence: The prevalence figure should be taken from Results and Fig 1, not the Abstract; it does not affect the odds ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample used for analysis is given as 150,010 drivers, but the four exposure groups add to 149,006; the other 1,004 (909 with two and 95 with three THC-positive tests) were left out of the primary analyses, and the 7,734 THC-positive drivers quoted in the Discussion equal 3,387 plus 4,347.
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary-analysis sample is 149,006 (editors' arithmetic); the paper's headline figure includes drivers used only in the secondary analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: Model 1 is described as run without adjustment for other factors, yet the Results label its odds ratios (1.11 for BAC, 1.28 for THC) as adjusted. They are adjusted for BAC terms only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The THC odds ratio adjusted for age, sex, other drugs and record is 1.165 (Table 2), not 1.28; the Highlights and Abstract use 16%.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusion say drivers positive for both agents had greater odds than drivers positive for either alone, but no test or interval is printed for the addition of THC to alcohol at BAC .05 or .08; Table 3 intervals for alcohol alone and for the combination are adjacent (1.63 to 1.69 against 1.70 to 1.93 at .05) or overlap (2.11 to 2.23 against 2.13 to 2.44 at .08). From the printed coefficients the added odds ratio for THC is about 1.09 at .05 and 1.05 at .08 (editors' calculation, no interval).
reporting_issues.consequence: How much THC adds to alcohol at legal-limit BAC is small and its precision is not given; the statement is better read as the combination being close to the sum of the single effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion speaks of the additive effect of cannabis at low BAC, but the model does not test additivity: the product term tests departure from multiplicative combination of odds ratios, and its odds ratio below 1 (0.987) shows a smaller-than-multiplicative combination. Close to additive is shown only by the editors' arithmetic on Table 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Additive and interaction are used for different things in the paper; no additive-scale test is reported.

reporting_issues.issue: Appendix 1 is cited for the comparison of tested and untested drivers and for a worked example of the predicted odds, and it is not in the manuscript PDF. Table 3's footnote gives only male drivers centered at age 45; the values of the other covariates are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selection into testing cannot be assessed from the manuscript; the other covariates are inferred (editors' check) to be at reference values.

reporting_issues.issue: The THC analyte (parent THC or a metabolite, such as the inactive carboxy-THC) and the detection limit are not stated, although the Discussion says THC can stay in the blood for hours or days. Eight FARS drug codes, including Marinol and hashish, count as THC.
reporting_issues.consequence: A THC-positive result may reflect use long before the crash; the authors attribute only underestimation to this.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give the sex difference as males having greater predicted odds than females, most pronounced in the youngest and oldest drivers. In Fig 2 (BAC 0, no THC; by eye) males are higher at age 25 (log odds about 0.56 against 0.37) but females are higher at 45 (about 0.11 against 0.07) and at 65 (about 0.41 against 0.29).
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the alcohol and THC estimates; Table 3 is for male drivers aged 45, where the sexes are closest.

reporting_issues.issue: The hypothesised fall in alcohol detection from 1993 to 2008, and the Abstract's examination of the prevalence of driving under the influence of alcohol, have no reported result; Fig 1 shows THC only.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not relevant to the odds ratios; one hypothesis is left without an answer.

Read: highlights, abstract, all sections, Tables 1 to 3, Figs 1 and 2, references and acknowledgements.
